options.C: Naloxone
options.D: Vitamin K

explanation: Naloxone is a lifesaver! It bumps opioids off their receptors in a hurry and helps the patient breathe again.

question: What is the main job of the foramen ovale in a baby before birth?

options.A: Connect the pulmonary artery directly to the aorta
options.B: Drain waste products directly into the umbilical vein
options.C: Supply oxygenated blood to the developing liver tissue
options.D: Shunt blood from the right atrium to the left atrium

explanation: Great job! Before birth, a baby's lungs aren't being used yet. The foramen ovale acts like a shortcut door between the upper heart chambers, letting oxygen-rich blood skip the resting lungs and head straight out to the body.

question: When food prices shoot up due to inflation, how do many families change what they eat?

options.A: They grow all their missing food requirements in backyard container gardens
options.B: They substitute nutrient-dense foods with cheaper, calorie-dense refined carbohydrates
options.C: They automatically increase their daily intake of fresh fruits and lean meats
options.D: They stop eating entirely until government food subsidies arrive in the mail

explanation: When money gets tight, families swap out expensive veggies and proteins for cheaper filler foods that fill the belly but lack vitamins.

question: A patient recovering from a bacterial gut infection comes back weeks later with painful, swollen joints. What is this likely called?

options.A: Septic joint infection
options.B: Rheumatoid arthritis
options.C: Reactive arthritis
options.D: Osteoarthritis

explanation: Spot on! The joints 'react' to the earlier gut infection with inflammation. You are really mastering these tricky complications!

question: Why are nurses such valuable members of a quality improvement team?

options.A: They write hospital policy manuals alone
options.B: They have formal training in hospital finance
options.C: They make all final administrative decisions
options.D: They spend the most time at the bedside

explanation: Exactly! Because nurses are right there with patients every day, they see firsthand what works and where things go wrong in clinical care.

question: When severe anxiety kicks off the 'fight-or-flight' response, which physical sign do you expect to see?

options.A: Constricted pupils
options.B: Slowed digestion with increased salivation
options.C: Decreased respiratory rate
options.D: Increased heart rate (tachycardia)

explanation: You got it! Adrenaline pumps through the body, making the heart beat fast and hard to get us ready to run or fight.

question: What is a major advantage of decentralising decisions down to frontline ward managers?

options.A: Complete standardisation of every hospital procedure
options.B: Faster response times to daily operational challenges on the ward
options.C: Lower salaries for all categories of nursing staff
options.D: Elimination of all policies set by top hospital administration

explanation: You got it! Letting ward leaders solve local problems on the spot means they don't have to wait around for approval from distant executives.

question: Why is it always smart to let a friend read your draft before you submit it?

options.A: It guarantees that your study will receive immediate funding
options.B: Writers often become blind to their own typographical and logical errors
options.C: Colleagues are legally required to rewrite the entire document for you
options.D: Peer review replaces the need for a formal methodology section

explanation: When you've stared at a paper for hours, typos hide from you! A fresh pair of eyes can spot little mistakes in seconds.

question: Which type of evaluation happens right along the way to give you feedback while you are still learning?

options.A: Formative evaluation
options.B: Diagnostic evaluation
options.C: Summative evaluation
options.D: Placement evaluation

explanation: Formative evaluation is like a practice quiz that helps 'form' or improve your skills while you are still learning.

question: Why is time considered so critical when dealing with emergency medical conditions?

options.A: Hospital regulations require fast bed turnover
options.B: Insurance companies will not pay for slow care
options.C: Doctors refuse to see patients who wait too long
options.D: Delays can lead to rapid deterioration and death

explanation: In critical emergencies, minutes matter because a failing body system quickly causes permanent harm or death if not supported. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T2#GNS315_U2_T2_h1)

question: Which infection is most directly linked to the development of cervical cancer?

options.A: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
options.B: Human papillomavirus
options.C: Chlamydia trachomatis
options.D: Human immunodeficiency virus

explanation: High-risk strains of human papillomavirus (HPV) can hang around in the cells of the cervix for years and eventually cause cell changes that lead to cancer.

question: You want villagers to remember proper handwashing steps after an outreach. What is the most practical action to take?

options.A: Distribute illustrated posters showing handwashing steps to take home or place in public areas
options.B: Write the medical names of bacteria on a chalkboard during a one-hour lecture
options.C: Tell the villagers to memorize the steps by repeating them three times in silence
options.D: Ask the village head to verbally test every single resident on handwashing theory

explanation: Pictures speak volumes! Visual posters give people a daily reminder so healthy hygiene habits actually stick.

question: A patient comes to the clinic with a cough lasting four weeks, drenching night sweats, and sudden weight loss. What should you suspect first?

options.A: Acute tension headache
options.B: Iron deficiency anemia
options.C: Simple seasonal allergy
options.D: Pulmonary tuberculosis

explanation: A long-standing cough, night sweats, and dropping weight without trying form the classic triad for active pulmonary TB. Great clinical spotting!

question: What physical examination technique involves using a stethoscope to listen to internal body sounds?

options.A: Palpation
options.B: Inspection
options.C: Percussion
options.D: Auscultation

explanation: Auscultation is the act of listening to sounds within the body, such as the heart and lungs, using a stethoscope. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T4#GNS124_U6_T4_h2)

question: Which ethical theory focuses strictly on creating the greatest good for the greatest number of people?

options.A: Classical control
options.B: Virtue ethics
options.C: Utilitarianism
options.D: Deontology

explanation: Think of utilitarianism as the 'greater good' approach. It weighs decisions based on which option brings the most overall benefit to the biggest group.

question: What are the three main parts of the epidemiological triangle?

options.A: Agent, host, and environment
options.B: Source, spread, and susceptibility
options.C: Bacteria, virus, and fungus
options.D: Vector, transmission, and portal

explanation: You nailed it! The epidemiological triangle consists of the infectious agent, the host who can catch it, and the environment where they meet.

question: Which special property sets a ratio scale apart from an interval scale?

options.A: The presence of unequal intervals between numbers
options.B: The use of categories that cannot be ranked
options.C: The complete absence of any numerical values
options.D: The presence of an absolute true zero point

explanation: A true zero means zero actually means none of that item exists (like 0 mL of urine output). That's what makes it a ratio scale!

question: A study tests if walking after surgery reduces hospital stay length. What is the dependent variable here?

options.A: The type of surgery performed
options.B: The nursing staff on duty
options.C: Walking after surgery
options.D: Length of the hospital stay

explanation: The dependent variable is the 'effect' or outcome you are measuring, which depends on the walking intervention.

question: A patient with a suspected ectopic pregnancy complains of sudden, sharp pain in her right shoulder. Why does this happen?

options.A: Anxiety is causing muscle tension in her upper body.
options.B: Blood in her pelvis has irritated her diaphragm.
options.C: She strained her shoulder muscle while feeling dizzy.
options.D: An infection has spread upward to her lungs.

explanation: This is a classic nursing nugget! Blood pooling in the belly can irritate the phrenic nerve, which shares pathways with the shoulder. That's why pain shows up there!

question: What is the main job of androgens (like testosterone) in the normal female body?

options.A: Stopping all activity in the anterior pituitary gland
options.B: Triggering immediate shedding of the uterine lining
options.C: Maintaining thick cervical mucus to block sperm entry
options.D: Supporting bone strength, libido, and serving as a precursor for estrogen

explanation: Even though they're often called 'male' hormones, women have them too! They keep your bones strong, fuel your energy and drive, and help build estrogen.

question: What crucial safety rule must be kept in mind when treating a patient infected with Taenia solium?

options.A: Giving the medication exclusively through an intravenous infusion
options.B: Ensuring the patient fasts completely for one week prior to dosing
options.C: Preventing the patient from swallowing shed eggs to avoid cysticercosis
options.D: Keeping the patient isolated in a negative pressure room

explanation: Brilliant! If the patient vomits or has poor hygiene during treatment, they might accidentally swallow T. solium eggs and develop dangerous tissue cysts.

question: What is the very first thing a nurse should do when turning an annoying ward problem into a research question?

options.A: Ordering expensive laboratory equipment for the ward
options.B: Reporting the nursing staff to the hospital board
options.C: Writing a textbook about the clinical problem
options.D: Focusing the observation onto clear, measurable variables

explanation: Start by breaking down your general frustration into specific pieces you can actually observe, count, or measure in the ward.

question: How does an autoclave primarily sterilize infectious waste?

options.A: By utilizing high-pressure, saturated steam to destroy pathogens
options.B: By exposing waste items to ultraviolet solar radiation for days
options.C: By burning organic materials into fine gray ash at very high heat
options.D: By dissolving plastic components in concentrated chemical solvents

explanation: Awesome! Autoclaves use pressurized steam to kill off stubborn germs effectively. You're mastering hospital equipment!

question: Why do heavy blocks of text usually fail in community health education programs?

options.A: People prefer listening to long audio recordings instead.
options.B: Ink tends to smudge when paragraphs are printed too close together.
options.C: Medical authorities forbid the use of written sentences on posters.
options.D: Low literacy rates in the target population make reading difficult.

explanation: Many community members have limited reading skills. If your poster is packed with heavy text, the main health message gets lost.

question: A patient who had a barium swallow two days ago reports no bowel movement, abdominal cramping, and bloating. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Immediate healing of an esophageal ulcer
options.B: A normal reaction to fasting before the test
options.C: Rapid absorption of contrast into the blood
options.D: Barium impaction leading to constipation

explanation: Barium dries out inside the large intestine, making constipation and impaction a major post-procedure risk if fluids and laxatives are not used. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T13#GNS221_U2_T13_h7)

question: Which two major veins join together to form the hepatic portal vein?

options.A: Superior mesenteric vein and splenic vein
options.B: Hepatic vein and inferior mesenteric vein
options.C: Internal jugular vein and subclavian vein
options.D: Inferior vena cava and renal vein

explanation: You'll find this intersection right behind the pancreas! The superior mesenteric vein and the splenic vein team up to form the hepatic portal vein carrying blood right to the liver.

question: Which part of the brain is the main control center for the vomiting reflex?

options.A: Cerebellum
options.B: Cerebral cortex
options.C: Hypothalamus
options.D: Medulla oblongata

explanation: Great job! The vomiting center sits right in the medulla oblongata of the brainstem, pulling together different nerve signals to trigger vomiting. You've got this!

question: What is the main difference between an additive interaction and a synergistic interaction?

options.A: Additive effects require three drugs, while synergistic effects only need two drugs
options.B: Synergistic effects are greater than the sum of separate effects, while additive effects equal the sum
options.C: Additive effects occur in the liver, while synergistic effects occur in the kidneys
options.D: Synergistic effects always cause dangerous toxicity, while additive effects are completely safe

explanation: Spot on! Additive is normal addition (1+1=2), while synergism is a multiplier effect where the total result punches above its weight class.

question: According to the Spaulding classification, how must you process a medical tool that goes deep inside sterile body tissues?

options.A: Simple soap washing
options.B: Sterilization
options.C: High-level disinfection
options.D: Low-level disinfection

explanation: If a tool enters sterile body tissues or blood vessels, it's a critical item and absolutely must be fully sterilized!

question: Why is it important to avoid heavy clinical jargon when reporting disaster monitoring data to non-medical coordinators?

options.A: To ensure disaster coordinators understand the message and act on it quickly
options.B: To make the report look less professional and more casual
options.C: Because clinical terms are illegal to use outside of hospital buildings
options.D: Because non-medical personnel are not allowed to hear health statistics

explanation: Clear, plain language prevents dangerous misunderstandings between health workers and municipal response teams. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h6)

question: Why do healthcare teams use structured improvement steps instead of just trying random ideas?

options.A: Random solutions take longer to write on paper
options.B: Structured frameworks are legally required for every shift change
options.C: Hospital management bans staff from making quick decisions
options.D: Random solutions rarely solve the root cause of the clinical problem

explanation: Spot on! When we use a structured approach, we dig deep to find the real cause of an issue rather than just guessing and hoping for the best.

question: What is the main purpose of a low-calorie diet?

options.A: Maximizing rapid muscle mass hypertrophy
options.B: Slowing down the basal metabolic rate
options.C: Increasing total daily physical endurance
options.D: Creating an energy deficit for weight loss

explanation: Spot on! A low-calorie diet simply means taking in fewer calories than your body burns, which forces it to use up stored fat for energy.

question: Why is it a mistake for a nurse manager to panic over every single normal, everyday variation?

options.A: It causes the hospital to lose its government license.
options.B: It creates unnecessary panic and wastes effort trying to fix a process that is working normally.
options.C: It forces staff to stop checking vital signs.
options.D: It instantly stops all new patient admissions to the ward.

explanation: Every day won't look identical. Overreacting to normal day-to-day fluctuations just stresses out the team for no reason!

question: What is the main job of motility inhibitor drugs in the gut?

options.A: Slow down gut movement to allow more water absorption
options.B: Coat the intestinal wall to prevent all nutrient uptake
options.C: Increase the speed of waste elimination
options.D: Kill infectious bacteria directly in the stomach

explanation: These drugs help calm down bowel movements. By slowing things down, your intestines get more time to soak up water from the stool.

question: In the SBAR communication tool, what does the letter 'R' stand for?

options.A: Recovery
options.B: Reassessment
options.C: Respiration
options.D: Recommendation

explanation: R is for Recommendation—this is where you clearly state what you think needs to happen next for the patient.

question: What is the main way that most foodborne germs get into our bodies?

options.A: Vector-borne transmission
options.B: Fecal-oral route
options.C: Direct sexual contact
options.D: Airborne droplet route

explanation: It sounds unpleasant, but tiny, microscopic traces of waste pathogens find their way onto food or water and enter right through the mouth. Handwashing is our best defense!

question: What is another popular name for cumulative incidence?

options.A: Incidence proportion
options.B: Attack density
options.C: Point prevalence
options.D: Mortality ratio

explanation: Easy peasy! Cumulative incidence is often called incidence proportion because it shows the proportion of the group that gets sick over time.

question: How many links make up the standard chain of infection?

options.A: Ten links
options.B: Six links
options.C: Four links
options.D: Eight links

explanation: You've got this! The chain of infection is made up of six links, starting from the infectious agent all the way to the susceptible host.

question: Why is local health research important for nurses in Nigeria?

options.A: Foreign textbooks are too expensive for local nursing students to buy
options.B: International organizations pay large grants exclusively to clinical nurses
options.C: Nigerian hospitals require every nurse to publish a paper before promotion
options.D: Western guidelines do not address specific local health challenges and cultural realities

explanation: You've got this! Local research matters because health issues like malaria management and maternal care need solutions tailored to our environment, rather than just copying foreign data. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T5#GNS217_U2_T5_h1)

question: You just finished charting on a ward computer. What is the most critical action to take right after?

options.A: Leave the charting screen open for the next shift
options.B: Turn off the computer monitor screen power
options.C: Print a physical copy of the screen for the desk
options.D: Log out of the computer session completely

explanation: Never leave your account open! Always log out completely so unauthorized people can't view or change patient info under your name.

question: An emergency patient needs medicine right now. Which route will work the fastest?

options.A: Intravenous
options.B: Topical cream
options.C: Oral capsule
options.D: Subcutaneous

explanation: You got it! IV is the champion for speed during emergencies because it enters the blood instantly.

question: Why do many families in Nigeria often turn to traditional care first when a loved one shows signs of mental illness?

options.A: Deep-rooted cultural philosophies and beliefs
options.B: Mandatory government healthcare policies
options.C: Strict orders from orthodox medical doctors
options.D: A complete absence of spiritual practices

explanation: You've got this! Cultural views deeply shape how communities understand illness, making traditional care a familiar and trusted first step for many families.

question: Why should you tell your patient NOT to bend their elbow right after getting blood drawn?

options.A: It forces the needle site to bleed faster than normal
options.B: It increases the risk of bruising and hematoma formation
options.C: It stops the remaining blood from flowing into the fingers
options.D: It causes the adhesive bandage to fall off the arm

explanation: Bending the arm puts pressure on the fresh puncture spot, which pops the clot loose and causes blood to leak underneath the skin into a nasty bruise.

question: A 45-year-old woman comes to the clinic with a hard, painless breast lump she noticed six months ago. What often causes this kind of late presentation in our communities?

options.A: Cultural stigma and trying alternative therapies first
options.B: The lump grew instantly overnight
options.C: Routine mammograms are done everywhere
options.D: The tumor was already surgically removed

explanation: Fear, stigma, and trying traditional remedies first are real barriers our patients face. As nurses, part of our job is compassionate, judgment-free education.

question: What is the primary benefit of involving local community leaders when planning a health education program?

options.A: It creates a sense of community ownership and cooperation
options.B: It allows the nurse to take a long holiday from clinical duties
options.C: It ensures the nurse receives a personal financial bonus
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for any teaching materials

explanation: When local leaders are involved from the start, the community is much more likely to trust the nurse and adopt the recommended health practices. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T1#GNS214_U1_T1_h4)

question: Which part of the brain acts as the body's natural thermostat during a fever?

options.A: Cerebellum
options.B: Hypothalamus
options.C: Thalamus
options.D: Medulla oblongata

explanation: The hypothalamus is like the internal thermostat in your brain. It turns up the heat when your body needs to fight off an infection.

question: Which of these is a part of the axial skeleton?

options.A: Pelvic girdle
options.B: Upper limb bones
options.C: Vertebral column
options.D: Pectoral girdle

explanation: The axial skeleton runs right down the middle—think skull, spine, and chest cage. You're doing great!

question: What is the deep cleaning process called that happens after an isolation patient is discharged?

options.A: Terminal cleaning
options.B: Standard wiping
options.C: Routine washing
options.D: Surface dusting

explanation: Terminal cleaning is the comprehensive disinfection of an entire room after a patient leaves, making it safe for the next occupant. [learn more](GST114_U2_T17#GST114_U2_T17_h6)

question: What is a major risk when a patient takes herbal supplements along with their regular prescription drugs?

options.A: Herbs always neutralize all side effects of drugs
options.B: Adverse drug-nutrient or herb-drug interactions
options.C: The prescription drugs will become completely odorless
options.D: The medications will instantly turn into sugar

explanation: Herbs are active chemicals too! When mixed with hospital drugs, they can sometimes clash, making the drugs too strong or blocking them from working.

question: What is a major result of a country having a high birth rate over many years?

options.A: A heavy economic dependency ratio with many young citizens
options.B: A rapid increase in the average age of the working population
options.C: An immediate shortage of geriatric care facilities
options.D: A permanent surplus of maternal hospital beds nationwide

explanation: Correct! High birth rates create a young population, meaning fewer working adults have to support many children.

question: Which of these is a safe and secure computer habit for clinical staff?

options.A: Sharing personal login passwords with trusted colleagues
options.B: Writing computer access codes on public office sticky notes
options.C: Leaving patient medical records open on unattended screens
options.D: Logging out of the computer workstation when leaving the desk

explanation: Always locking your screen or logging out keeps patient data safe from prying eyes when you step away. Great habit to build early! [learn more](GNS113_U1_T8#GNS113_U1_T8_h5)

question: What is the main goal of doing a dietary assessment in a community?

options.A: To understand the regular food intake and eating patterns of families
options.B: To calculate the exact financial income of every household
options.C: To determine the water sanitation index of the village
options.D: To diagnose infectious diseases like malaria and typhoid

explanation: Great! By asking about what families normally eat, nurses can spot missing nutrients and help plan practical solutions. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T7#GNS313_U3_T7_h5)

question: In the out-of-hospital chain of survival, what comes right after recognizing the emergency and calling for help?

options.A: Post-resuscitation care
options.B: Early CPR
options.C: Early defibrillation
options.D: Advanced life support

explanation: You've got this! After calling for help, getting hands on the chest for early CPR is the next vital step to keep blood moving.

question: Why is client-centered contraceptive counselling so important during post-abortion care?

options.A: It forces the client to use surgical sterilization
options.B: It helps the client freely choose a method that fits her life
options.C: It reduces the amount of paperwork for the clinic
options.D: It guarantees that the client will never need healthcare again

explanation: Client-centered care respects autonomy. We help her pick a method that matches her personal lifestyle and goals without pressure or judgment. [learn more](GNS226_U5_T007#GNS226_U5_T007_h5)

question: Why is giving a patient a regular bath or helping them wash up so important in the ward?

options.A: It prevents skin breakdown and infections
options.B: It helps the patient get discharged faster
options.C: It stops doctors from doing morning rounds
options.D: It reduces hospital drug bills

explanation: You're doing great! Regular hygiene washes away harmful germs and dead skin cells, keeping pressure sores and infections far away from your patient.

question: As an IEC implementer in a community clinic, what is one of the nurse's main jobs?

options.A: Educating patients during routine care and outreach sessions
options.B: Constructing physical buildings for the local health center
options.C: Manufacturing pharmaceutical drugs for distribution
options.D: Enforcing legal penalties for ignoring health advice

explanation: Everyday clinic visits, immunizations, and community outreaches are golden opportunities for nurses to teach and counsel patients. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T9#GNS124_U5_T9_h6)

question: Why did Florence Nightingale use visual diagrams like her famous polar area chart?

options.A: To hide negative hospital statistics from military generals
options.B: To predict future disease outbreaks in European cities
options.C: To make complex data easy for non-medical leaders to understand
options.D: To decorate official reports for the royal family

explanation: Visual charts helped politicians and military commanders quickly grasp the shocking death toll caused by poor hygiene rather than battle wounds. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T3#GNS217_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why do lipid-soluble (steroid) hormones need carrier proteins to travel through the blood?

options.A: To speed up their breakdown by the liver and kidneys
options.B: Because blood plasma is mostly water and they do not mix well
options.C: To help them actively destroy harmful pathogens in the blood
options.D: Because they are too large to pass through capillary walls

explanation: Oil and water don't mix! Since blood plasma is mostly water, these fat-based steroid hormones need a carrier protein to hitch a ride and travel safely through circulation.

question: Why do traditional NSAIDs often give patients a grumpy stomach or ulcers after long-term use?

options.A: They block COX-1, which removes the protective lining of the stomach
options.B: They increase the production of stomach acid to dangerous levels
options.C: They directly burn the stomach wall upon contact
options.D: They stop the stomach from digesting food properly

explanation: Not all prostaglandins are bad! COX-1 makes a special lining that protects your tummy from its own acid. When NSAIDs block COX-1, that protective shield gets thin. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T4#GNS223_U5_T4_h1)

question: How should the weights attached to Gallows traction hang?

options.A: Hanging freely without touching the floor or bed
options.B: Resting gently on the edge of the mattress
options.C: Adjusted by parents every few hours
options.D: Touching the floor for stability

explanation: Weights need to swing completely free in the air to give the exact pulling force required. If they touch the floor, the weight is off!

question: What is the replacement-level fertility rate needed to keep a population stable over time?

options.A: 2.1 children per woman
options.B: 1.0 child per woman
options.C: 4.5 children per woman
options.D: 6.0 children per woman

explanation: A fertility rate of roughly 2.1 children per woman means each generation replaces itself nicely without causing the population to surge or shrink too fast.

question: What is the primary nature of psychological trauma experienced during a disaster?

options.A: A permanent mental illness in all survivors
options.B: A normal reaction to an abnormal situation
options.C: A physical injury requiring immediate surgery
options.D: A sign of personal weakness or poor upbringing

explanation: Trauma responses are standard human reactions when faced with terrifying, life-threatening events beyond normal daily experience. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T6#GNS315_U5_T6_h1)

question: What do we call a specific patch of skin that gets its nerve supply from just one spinal nerve?

options.A: Ganglion
options.B: Funiculus
options.C: Myotome
options.D: Dermatome

explanation: Brilliant! A dermatome is just a skin map. 'Derma' means skin, and each segment corresponds to a specific spinal nerve pair checking in on that area.

question: Which type of FGM involves removing the clitoris along with part or all of the labia minora?

options.A: Type I FGM
options.B: Type II FGM
options.C: Type IV FGM
options.D: Type III FGM

explanation: You've got this! Type II FGM is also called excision, where both the clitoris and labia minora are removed.

question: Why do food safety officers frequently inspect local open-air markets and street food vendors?

options.A: These vendors feed a huge portion of the urban working-class population
options.B: Street vendors have more money to pay official fines
options.C: Open markets never have contamination problems
options.D: Large supermarkets are legally exempt from all safety checks

explanation: Since millions of people buy from local markets and street vendors every day, keeping those foods safe is crucial for public health.

question: What is the main goal of a Root Cause Analysis (RCA) after something goes wrong in the hospital?

options.A: Calculating the financial cost of lost equipment
options.B: Finding a junior nurse to blame and dismissing them immediately
options.C: Hiding the incident from the hospital management board
options.D: Discovering underlying system flaws that allowed the error to happen

explanation: RCA doesn't look for someone to point a finger at; it digs deep into the system to fix broken processes so it never happens again.

question: What is your absolute first priority when managing a patient with acute upper airway trauma?

options.A: Giving pain relief medications
options.B: Stopping external bleeding with tight bandages
options.C: Securing and maintaining a clear airway
options.D: Taking a detailed medical history

explanation: Spot on! Airway management always comes first in trauma care to make sure the patient gets enough oxygen before anything else.

question: A disease spreads rapidly across several countries and continents. What is this global event called?

options.A: Endemic
options.B: Hyperendemic
options.C: Pandemic
options.D: Holoendemic

explanation: A pandemic is an epidemic that has spread over a very wide area, crossing international borders to affect multiple countries or continents. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T14#GNS313_U1_T14_h2)

question: Why must nurse leaders assess the current environment before trying to change the culture?

options.A: To comply with building safety codes and fire regulations
options.B: To find out which individual staff members need immediate firing
options.C: To gather baseline data and identify specific problem areas
options.D: To calculate the exact budget required for annual staff bonuses

explanation: You're right! Assessment helps leaders see what's really happening so they can target actual problems rather than just guessing.

question: When does the immediate puerperium period happen?

options.A: Between the second and sixth week
options.B: Before the placenta is delivered
options.C: The first 24 hours after delivery
options.D: The entire first week after birth

explanation: Spot on! The immediate puerperium covers the first 24 hours post-delivery. As nurses, we watch new mums closely during this window because the risk for heavy bleeding is at its highest.

question: How should a nurse respond to a patient who insists on getting an injection instead of pills for a mild illness?

options.A: Explain that oral medications are often just as effective and much safer
options.B: Tell the patient that injections are illegal for treating mild illnesses
options.C: Refuse to speak with the patient until they accept the prescribed pills
options.D: Administer a harmless saline injection to satisfy their psychological need

explanation: Patient education works best when it's kind and respectful. Clear up the myth about injections while highlighting why safe oral meds are great.

question: What term describes an infant's inborn, natural mood and emotional reactivity?

options.A: Psyche
options.B: Consciousness
options.C: Delusion
options.D: Temperament

explanation: Temperament refers to the biologically rooted behavioral and emotional traits that babies are born with. [learn more](GNS314_U1_T8#GNS314_U1_T8_h3)

question: What is a primary immunodeficiency disorder?

options.A: Something that only affects adults over sixty
options.B: An issue triggered by common painkillers
options.C: An inherited genetic defect present right from birth
options.D: A condition caused by severe physical trauma later in life

explanation: Think of 'primary' as being born with it. These disorders stem from gene mutations passed down from parents, unlike secondary ones that happen later in life.

question: Which hormone is released by special cells in the heart when the heart walls get stretched too much?

options.A: Melatonin
options.B: Renin
options.C: Erythropoietin
options.D: Atrial natriuretic peptide

explanation: When your heart chambers are stretched by high blood volume, they release Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP) to tell your kidneys to get rid of extra water and salt, helping lower your blood pressure.

question: A nurse creates a care plan focusing on a patient's personal goals, past trauma, and community support. What approach is this?

options.A: The demonological approach to mental illness
options.B: Colonial-era prison management models
options.C: Trauma-informed and recovery-oriented care
options.D: Custodial asylum containment strategies

explanation: Modern nursing looks at the whole human being! We combine trauma awareness with a recovery mindset instead of just trying to quiet down symptoms.

question: Why do most nurses love using the formula method for drug calculations?

options.A: It is a straightforward, reliable way to figure out the required dose
options.B: It automatically converts pounds to kilograms without math
options.C: It eliminates the need to ever verify orders with the pharmacist
options.D: It works exclusively for intravenous medications

explanation: You got it! The 'Desired over Have' formula gives you a clear, easy-to-remember shortcut for your daily clinical math.

question: What is the main nutritional catch of relying on just one single staple food, like only eating cassava for every meal?

options.A: It provides zero calories needed for daily physical activity
options.B: It lacks a complete profile of essential proteins and fats
options.C: It causes immediate and severe vitamin toxicity in adults
options.D: It contains too much dietary fiber for the human stomach

explanation: Spot on! While staples give great energy, eating only one thing leaves big gaps in other vital nutrients. Variety is always key!

question: You cannot feel a dying patient's radial pulse at the wrist. What should you do next as the nurse?

options.A: Call the doctor immediately to start IV fluids
options.B: Apply a warm water bottle to their hands
options.C: Pump the blood pressure cuff higher on their arm
options.D: Check a central pulse like the carotid or femoral

explanation: When peripheral circulation gets weak, wrist pulses fade first. Checking a central pulse helps you accurately check the remaining heart activity. You're building great clinical instincts!

question: Which layer of the epidermis is busy making new skin cells and producing melanin for color?

options.A: Stratum basale
options.B: Stratum corneum
options.C: Stratum granulosum
options.D: Stratum spinosum

explanation: You got it! The stratum basale is the deepest layer of the epidermis where cell division happens constantly, and special cells called melanocytes make our skin pigment.

question: What does a dermatome represent in physical assessment?

options.A: A reflex arc located in the lower spine
options.B: The protective covering around the spinal cord
options.C: An area of skin supplied by a single spinal nerve
options.D: A group of muscles controlled by one motor nerve

explanation: A dermatome is a skin segment that receives its sensory innervation from one specific spinal nerve. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T26#GNS211_U3_T26_h8)

question: What is drug antagonism in plain terms?

options.A: Two drugs combine to create a much larger therapeutic effect
options.B: Plasma protein binding sites become overloaded with free drug
options.C: One drug blocks or counteracts the effect of another drug
options.D: Liver enzymes speed up the clearance of both medications

explanation: Imagine two kids fighting over a single chair. Antagonism is when one drug jumps onto a cell receptor and blocks another substance from getting in or working!

question: A newly admitted patient gets dizzy from medications and has a history of stumbling. What should you do first?

options.A: Keep the patient strictly confined to a wheelchair
options.B: Restrict all fluid intake to prevent bathroom trips
options.C: Order physical therapy to cure the dizziness immediately
options.D: Implement a targeted fall prevention care plan

explanation: Well done! Spotting risk factors early means you can put safety measures in place before the patient takes a tumble.

question: What is the main purpose of translational research in nursing?

options.A: To move lab discoveries into actual bedside patient care
options.B: To change hospital policies without any scientific proof
options.C: To translate foreign medical books into local languages
options.D: To convert qualitative interviews into numerical charts

explanation: You're doing great! Translational research helps bridge the gap between science discoveries in a lab and everyday clinical practice so patients benefit faster. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T4#GNS217_U1_T4_h6)

question: A hospital safety committee has limited funds and must fix hazards. Which risk should they tackle first?

options.A: A frequent risk that can cause permanent patient disability
options.B: A rare risk that causes a minor inconvenience to visitors
options.C: A paperwork delay that does not affect direct patient care
options.D: A one-time complaint about the taste of the drinking water

explanation: Risks with high frequency and severe consequences demand immediate action to prevent serious patient harm. [learn more](GST319_U4_T6#GST319_U4_T6_h3)

question: Why is it important to separate a medical error from an unavoidable adverse event?

options.A: Adverse events always lead to immediate legal action against the nurse
options.B: Medical errors only happen in surgical wards, while adverse events happen in clinics
options.C: Unavoidable adverse events are always caused by nurse negligence
options.D: Errors involve preventable mistakes, while some adverse events are known risks of treatment

explanation: Recognizing the difference helps teams identify what could have been prevented versus what was an unpredictable reaction to care. [learn more](GST319_U6_T1#GST319_U6_T1_h1)

question: When does the highest risk for postpartum hemorrhage and maternal death happen?

options.A: During the fourth month after delivery
options.B: Within the first 48 hours after childbirth
options.C: Two weeks before labor starts
options.D: At the final six-week checkup

explanation: That's right! The first 48 hours after birth are the most critical window for watching out for sudden, dangerous bleeding and infections.

question: Why is community health nursing so important to primary health care in Nigeria?

options.A: It manages all tertiary hospital admissions across the country
options.B: It brings preventative and basic health services directly to local populations
options.C: It exclusively handles complex surgical procedures in rural areas
options.D: It replaces the need for doctors in government hospitals

explanation: You got it! By stepping into local clinics, schools, and homes, community health nurses make sure everyday preventative care actually reaches where people live.

question: Why is it important for a nurse researcher to know about different scales of measurement?

options.A: To calculate the exact financial cost of a hospital ward
options.B: To determine which nurses get promoted to head nurse
options.C: To bypass the hospital ethics committee approval process
options.D: To select the correct statistical tests for data analysis

explanation: Different types of data need different mathematical tools. Knowing your measurement scale helps you pick the right statistical test to make sense of your findings.

question: What is a common reason adolescent girls miss or drop out of school once they reach puberty?

options.A: Mandatory government laws prohibiting teenagers from studying science
options.B: Complete lack of interest in academic subjects after primary education
options.C: Sudden loss of intellectual capacity related to biological changes
options.D: Lack of private sanitation facilities and affordable menstrual products

explanation: Sadly, many girls miss classes because their schools lack clean, private toilets or affordable pads to manage their periods comfortably.

question: What does the top number in a blood pressure reading represent?

options.A: Systolic pressure during heart contraction
options.B: Diastolic pressure during heart relaxation
options.C: Mean arterial pressure across the cardiac cycle
options.D: Central venous pressure inside the right atrium

explanation: The systolic (top) number measures the peak pressure in your arteries when the heart pumps. You're mastering the basics! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h5)

question: Why is it important for home health nurses to check in on the family caregiver's health too?

options.A: If the caregiver falls ill, the entire home care arrangement can collapse.
options.B: Caregivers are legally responsible for writing medical prescriptions.
options.C: Family members are the primary patients receiving nursing therapy.
options.D: Hospital regulations require checking caregiver blood pressure weekly.

explanation: Spot on! The patient's safety at home relies heavily on the health and well-being of the person taking care of them.

question: Why is it sometimes a bad idea to immediately stop infectious diarrhoea with medicine?

options.A: It permanently destroys the muscles of the colon
options.B: It completely stops the absorption of all vitamins
options.C: It traps harmful toxins and bacteria inside the gut
options.D: It causes an immediate spike in blood pressure

explanation: When germs cause diarrhoea, your body tries to flush them out. Stopping the flow too soon just keeps the bad stuff trapped inside you!

question: What is the primary reason for completely exposing a trauma patient during the primary survey?

options.A: To prepare the patient for a routine bed bath
options.B: To cool down a patient with a high fever
options.C: To find hidden injuries or bleeding sites
options.D: To make it easier to apply ECG monitoring leads

explanation: Full exposure allows the nurse to inspect the entire body for concealed wounds, fractures, or bleeding that require urgent care. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T8#GNS112_U7_T8_h7)

question: As a student nurse, how often should you check and inspect an active peripheral IV site on your patient?

options.A: Once every 48 hours during dressing changes
options.B: Only when the patient complains of severe pain
options.C: Only when the infusion bag runs completely empty
options.D: At least once every nursing shift

explanation: Exactly! Regular checks each shift help you catch tiny problems like early swelling or soreness before they turn into bigger issues.

question: What is the main goal of medical treatment during the early and middle stages of this disease?

options.A: Completely curing the underlying genetic defect
options.B: Slowing disease progression and managing blood pressure
options.C: Regenerating completely healthy new kidney tissue
options.D: Stopping all urine production to rest the body

explanation: Since kidney scarring cannot be undone, the primary goal of treatment is to protect the nephrons we have left and keep the patient stable for as long as possible.

question: Within what window of time should standard levonorgestrel emergency pills be taken for the best result?

options.A: Within 14 days of unprotected intercourse
options.B: At any time during the entire monthly cycle
options.C: Exactly 24 hours after the next menstrual period
options.D: Within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse

explanation: Levonorgestrel (like the popular Postinor-2) works best when taken within 72 hours (3 days) after unprotected sex. Keep this rule of thumb handy!

question: What does a high Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) usually tell you about a patient?

options.A: Excessive bone mineral density
options.B: Decreased red blood cell production
options.C: Active inflammation or infection
options.D: Low dietary calcium intake

explanation: When there is inflammation in the body, certain proteins make red blood cells stick together and fall faster in a test tube. That speeds up the ESR! Spotting this helps you catch inflammation early.

question: Which action should a nurse take when conducting a mental health screening in a community clinic?

options.A: Build trusting rapport and explain the purpose of the screening questions
options.B: Diagnosing the patient with a psychiatric disorder immediately on the spot
options.C: Rushing through the questions so the patient does not feel uncomfortable
options.D: Ignoring non-verbal cues and focusing strictly on the written score

explanation: Establishing trust and explaining the purpose of screening helps reduce anxiety and encourages honest answers from the patient. [learn more](GNS314_U5_T1#GNS314_U5_T1_h6)

question: How do you know if a data collection tool (like a questionnaire) is truly valid?

options.A: It accurately measures what it is intended to measure
options.B: It has been approved by the hospital accountant
options.C: It is extremely cheap to print and distribute
options.D: It takes less than two minutes for patients to finish

explanation: Validity just means your tool does the job it's supposed to do—it's actually testing the specific variable you care about.

question: What is the correct rhythm of compressions to breaths when resuscitating a newborn?

options.A: 15 compressions to 2 breaths
options.B: 3 compressions to 1 breath
options.C: 30 compressions to 2 breaths
options.D: 5 compressions to 1 breath

explanation: For newborns, we use a 3 to 1 ratio (3 compressions followed by 1 breath) to give both heart support and oxygen.

question: Why are people with long-term leg swelling at higher risk for skin infections like cellulitis?

options.A: Swollen legs attract insects that transmit bacterial infections.
options.B: Increased blood flow carries too many white blood cells to the skin.
options.C: Fluid buildup inside the tissues directly manufactures harmful bacteria.
options.D: Stretched, fragile skin easily develops cracks that let bacteria enter.

explanation: Exactly! When skin is constantly stretched out by fluid, it gets dry, thin, and fragile. Tiny cracks form easily, giving bacteria an easy doorway in.

question: How does actively absorbing sodium from the gut affect fluid movement?

options.A: It destroys water molecules to prevent severe dehydration
options.B: It draws water out of the lumen and into the mucosal cells
options.C: It repels water molecules and forces them into the stool
options.D: It keeps water trapped inside the lumen until digestion finishes

explanation: Exactly! Pumping sodium out of the gut space creates an osmotic pull that drags water right along with it into the body tissues.

question: What is a major drawback of rapid bolus tube feedings?

options.A: They must run continuously for the entire day
options.B: They require expensive electronic pump machinery
options.C: They can cause nausea, cramping, and fullness
options.D: They completely eliminate normal bowel sounds

explanation: Pouring a large volume of formula into the stomach too fast overwhelms the organ, frequently leading to abdominal discomfort and vomiting. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h4)

question: Why do patients with chronic hookworm infections often develop anemia?

options.A: Suppression of bone marrow by parasite toxins
options.B: Rapid destruction of red blood cells by the liver
options.C: A complete lack of dietary protein intake
options.D: Ongoing blood loss from intestinal attachment

explanation: Hookworms latch onto the inside of the intestines and feed on the host's blood. Over time, this steady loss adds up and leads to anemia. Makes total sense when you picture it!

question: How can a nurse manager best handle frequent equipment shortages during daily ward activities?

options.A: Refuse to admit any new patients until funding improves
options.B: Blame the junior nurses for failing to improvise supplies
options.C: Ignore the missing equipment and ask patients to buy everything
options.D: Maximise available resources and advocate for better supply systems

explanation: You're thinking like a true leader! A great manager makes the best of what's on hand while constantly pushing upper management for better supplies.

question: Why does a Root Cause Analysis look beyond individual staff error?

options.A: Because government laws forbid blaming nurses for bad patient outcomes
options.B: Because hospital managers want to protect nurses from losing their licenses
options.C: Because most errors are caused by weak systems, equipment flaws, or poor processes
options.D: Because individual mistakes are impossible to prove in a court of law

explanation: RCA looks at the big picture because fixing a broken system prevents future errors much better than simply blaming a worker. [learn more](GST319_U4_T6#GST319_U4_T6_h5)

question: Why is an elevated pulse often considered an early warning sign of patient distress?

options.A: The heart speeds up to compensate before blood pressure drops
options.B: Fever always causes immediate kidney failure if left untreated
options.C: It proves the patient is simply feeling nervous about hospital food
options.D: A fast pulse means the lungs have stopped absorbing oxygen entirely

explanation: The body increases the heart rate to maintain adequate blood flow and pressure when stress, blood loss, or illness occurs. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T8#GNS111_U2_T8_h6)

question: Why is using frayed electrical cords dangerous?

options.A: They stop household light bulbs from working
options.B: Damaged cords pull too much electricity from the grid
options.C: Exposed wires can cause electric shock or fire
options.D: Frayed wires release toxic gases into the room

explanation: When insulation wears away, bare wires can spark against furniture or skin, causing burns or electrical shocks. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T4#GNS324_U6_T4_h7)

question: Why does poor nutrition often lead to longer hospital stays for sick patients?

options.A: It slows down wound healing and weakens the immune system.
options.B: It automatically lowers the patient's daily hospital fees.
options.C: It forces the hospital kitchen to prepare special meals.
options.D: It stops the patient from sleeping during the night.

explanation: When a body lacks proper nutrients, tissue repair slows down and fighting off secondary infections becomes much harder, delaying recovery. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T023#GNS227_U2_T023_h1)

question: Why do nurses treat Wernicke encephalopathy as a true emergency?

options.A: It triggers sudden high blood pressure that never responds to drugs
options.B: It can cause quick, permanent brain damage if treatment is delayed
options.C: It quickly spreads as a contagious infection
options.D: It causes immediate paralysis in all four limbs

explanation: You got it! Because it affects the brain so fast, replacing thiamine right away is crucial to prevent lasting harm.
